chunks: I was told by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: We were told by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab, from Ghiyath ibn Kalub, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his fathers, peace be upon them, that he said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his Family, said:

What you find in the Book of Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, the (dutiful) act for you is in it; there is no excuse for you to abandon it. What is not in the Book of Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, and about which there is a Tradition from me, there is no excuse for you to abandon my Tradition. That which there is no Tradition from me about, then whatever my companions say, you say (likewise), for indeed, the example of my companions among you is only like the example of the stars; whichever of them is taken, one is guided, and by whichever saying of my companions you take, you will be guided. The dissimilarity between my companions among you is a mercy. Then it was said: O Messenger of Allah, and who are your companions? He said: My Household.
ai.seo_question: Who are the companions of the Prophet according to this hadith from Ma'ani al-Akhbar?
ai.summary: This hadith from Maani al-Akhbar establishes a clear hierarchy of religious authority, culminating in the identification of the Prophet's 'companions' (Sahaba) specifically as his Ahl al-Bayt, a key Shia interpretation that distinguishes them from the broader community. The metaphor of the stars signifies that while the Ahl al-Bayt possess infallible guidance, their scholarly differences (ikhtilaf) serve as a mercy (rahma) by providing flexibility in legal application. This text underscores the Shia view that the Prophet's family is the ultimate source of post-Quranic authority and jurisprudential diversity.
